question: How does Paul introduce himself, what does he say about the Son of God, and how does he describe the recipients in Rome?
Paul did not yet know the church in Rome: what reasons does he give for wanting to visit it, and what does it mean that he calls himself “obligated” to Greeks and barbarians?
The word εὐαγγέλιον (euangelion, “gospel, good news”) appears in the verse many consider the theme of the letter: what does Paul say the gospel is, and what is revealed in it?

What sequence does Paul describe between knowing God, not glorifying Him and being “given over” by God Himself, and how do the Christian traditions discuss the application of parts of this list today?
“I am not ashamed of the gospel”: in what setting do you feel shame or fear about showing what you believe?
To whom does Paul now speak with “you who pass judgment,” and what accusation does he make against this imaginary conversation partner?
How does Paul describe the Gentiles who do not have the Law but show “the work of the Law written on their hearts,” and what role does he give to conscience?

The word περιτομή (peritome, “circumcision”) appears at the end of the chapter together with the idea of “circumcision of the heart”: what distinction does Paul make between the outward sign and the inward one?
“You, then, who teach others, do you not teach yourself?”: at what point is what you demand of others not yet fulfilled in you?
What questions and objections does Paul raise right at the beginning of the chapter, and how does he answer each one?
Why does Paul gather so many quotations from Scripture to conclude that all, Jews and Greeks, are “under sin”?

The word ἱλαστήριον (hilasterion), translated here as “atoning sacrifice,” is also rendered “propitiation” or “expiation”: what does each translation highlight, and what Old Testament image does it evoke?
If boasting is excluded and justification is by faith, why does Paul insist that this does not nullify the Law but upholds it?
Paul says that “all have sinned” and that they are justified “freely”: how do these two statements together affect the way you see yourself and others?
At what moment in Abraham's life was faith credited to him as righteousness, before or after circumcision, and what conclusion does Paul draw from this?
The verb λογίζομαι (logizomai, “credit, reckon, count”) is repeated throughout the chapter: what image of bookkeeping does it bring, and how does Paul apply it to Abraham and to “us”?
In what sense is Abraham “the father of us all,” and why does Paul say the promise must be “by faith” in order to be “by grace”?
Abraham “believed, against all hope,” looking at his own aging body: what promise or hope do you find hard to hold onto when you look at the circumstances?
What consequences of justification by faith does Paul list at the beginning of the chapter, and what sequence does he trace starting from sufferings?
The verb καταλλάσσω (katallasso, “reconcile”) presupposes a broken relationship: who is reconciled with whom, according to these verses, and in what condition were they before?
What parallel does Paul draw between Adam and Christ, and why does he repeat the phrase “how much more” so often?
God shows His love “while we were still sinners”: how does this order of events change the way you approach God on the days you feel unworthy?
What objection does Paul anticipate at the very beginning of the chapter, and what is his immediate answer?

The verb βαπτίζω (baptizo, “baptize, immerse”) appears linked to death and burial with Christ: what image does Paul build here, and how do the Christian traditions relate this passage to the practice of baptism?
Paul says everyone is a slave of someone: what distinguishes being a slave of sin from being a slave of righteousness, and why does he use such a strong image?
Paul asks us to present the “members” of the body as instruments of righteousness: what concrete part of your routine (hands, words, eyes, time) needs this surrender?
What example does Paul use about marriage and the husband's death, and what does he want to illustrate with it?
If the Law is “holy, righteous and good,” how does sin manage to use the commandment to produce death?
The word νόμος (nomos, “law”) appears in several senses in the chapter, as God's Law and as “another law” in the members: how can we distinguish these senses when reading verses 21 to 25?
Who is the “I” who does not do the good he wants: Paul before Christ, the Christian in struggle, or a figure of Israel? What clues does the text offer for each reading?
“What a wretched man I am! Who will rescue me?”: in what inner struggle do you recognize yourself in this sentence, and where does Paul find the way out?
How many times is the Spirit mentioned in the first eleven verses, and what contrast does Paul draw between the mind of the flesh and that of the Spirit?

The word υἱοθεσία (huiothesia, “adoption as sons”) appears in the cry “Abba, Father” and in the waiting for the redemption of the body: why does Paul speak of adoption as something already received and still awaited?
What does it mean that the whole creation groans “as in the pains of childbirth,” and what relationship does Paul see between the future of God's children and the future of the created world?
The verbs “foreknew, predestined, called, justified, glorified” form a chain: how do the different Christian traditions usually understand this passage?
Paul lists what cannot separate us from God's love: what would you add to this list from your fears of today?
With what emotion does Paul open this part of the letter, and what privileges does he list as belonging to the Israelites?
Paul says “the word of God” has not failed: what distinction does he make between the children of the flesh and the children of the promise, using the stories of Isaac, Jacob and Esau?

The verb ἐλεέω (eleeo, “have mercy”) dominates the answer to the objection about God's justice: what does Paul affirm about mercy, and how do the Christian traditions read the image of the potter that comes right after?
Paul says he could wish himself cut off from Christ for the sake of his kinsmen: for whom do you carry a similar sorrow, and how does it show up in your prayers?
What does Paul ask of God for Israel, and how does he describe the zeal he recognizes in his people?
The word τέλος (telos) in “Christ is the end of the Law” can mean termination, goal or fulfillment: what difference does each of these senses make in reading the verse?
What chain of questions does Paul build from “call on” to “be sent,” and what does it say about how faith reaches people?
“The word is near you; it is in your mouth and in your heart”: what relationship is there in your life between what you believe inwardly and what you declare aloud?
What proofs does Paul present that God has not rejected His people, beginning with himself and the story of Elijah?
The verb ἐγκεντρίζω (enkentrizo, “graft in”) supports the image of the olive tree: who is the cultivated olive tree, who is the wild branch, and what warning does Paul give the Gentiles from this?
What does Paul call a “mystery,” and what might “all Israel will be saved” mean? How have interpreters of different traditions read this phrase?
Why does a long argument end in a hymn of praise, and what does this ending say about the way Paul does theology?
“Do not boast... you do not support the root”: how can remembering the Jewish root of the Christian faith change your attitude?
What does Paul ask of the brothers in the first two verses, and on what does he base this request?
The verb μεταμορφόω (metamorphoo, “transform”) appears in contrast with “conforming” to this age: what does Paul say must be renewed for this transformation to happen?
How does the image of the body with many members help Paul speak of the different gifts, and what attitude does he expect of each one toward their own gift?
What meaning might the image of “heaping burning coals” on the enemy's head have, in the context of not taking revenge?
Of the many short exhortations of verses 9 to 16, which is hardest for you to live out today, and why?
What reasons does Paul give for every person to be subject to the authorities, and what concrete duties does he mention?

The word ἐξουσία (exousia, “authority”) is repeated at the beginning of the chapter: how should we read these verses alongside texts like Acts 5:29, and what limits to this submission have Christians seen throughout history?
Why does Paul say love is the one debt that is never paid off, and how does he sum up the commandments?
“The night is nearly over; the day has drawn near”: what “deeds of darkness” do you need to lay aside, and what would it mean for you to “put on” Christ today?
What differences in practice among the brothers does Paul describe, and what does he ask of the one who eats and the one who does not?
What argument does Paul use to take away from the brothers the right to judge one another in these matters?
The word πρόσκομμα (proskomma, “stumbling block, obstacle”) appears when Paul speaks of the freedom to eat: what limit does he place on his own freedom, and why?
“The kingdom of God is not a matter of eating and drinking, but of righteousness, peace and joy”: on what secondary issue have you been spending energy that could go to peace and building up?
What example of Christ does Paul use to ask the strong to bear with the weak, and what is the central request of verse 7?
The verb προσλαμβάνω (proslambano, “accept, welcome”) takes up the beginning of chapter 14: what does it mean to accept one another “just as Christ accepted you”?
Why does Paul string together so many quotations about the Gentiles praising God, and how does this close the argument about Jews and Gentiles in the letter?
What travel plans does Paul present, and why is the collection for the poor in Jerusalem so important to him?
Paul asks the brothers to “struggle” with him in prayer: whom could you invite to pray with you for something difficult, or for whom could you struggle in prayer?
How many people does Paul greet, how many are women, and what expressions does he use to describe the work of each one?
Phoebe is called διάκονος (diakonos, “servant, deaconess, minister”) of the church in Cenchrea: how have translations and the Christian traditions understood this word and Phoebe's role?
Why, in the middle of the greetings, does Paul give a warning about those who cause divisions, and how does he describe these people?
Prisca and Aquila risked their lives for Paul and opened their house to the church: whom would you recognize by name, as Paul does here, for what they have done for you and for the community?
